title: The Impact of Technology
summary: Positive and negative impacts of technology on people, society and the environment, bias in technology, ethics, sustainability and evaluating products.

notes.text: Every technological product has **impacts**, both intended and unintended, on people, society, the economy and the environment. Technologists must think about these impacts when they design.

rows: Instant communication, banking, learning and emergency help
Cyberbullying, addiction, e-waste, distraction while driving
Fast transport of people and goods
Air pollution, accidents, traffic congestion, fossil-fuel use
Reliable electricity for homes and industry
Air pollution, acid rain, greenhouse gases, water use
Litter, ocean pollution, made from oil
Faster, safer and more accurate production

notes.text: When a product favours some groups of people over others, or excludes some groups, often without the designer intending it.

items: **Gender bias**: tools sized for men's hands; safety gear designed for male body shapes.
**Age bias**: small text and complex menus that older people find hard to use.
**Disability bias**: buildings without ramps; websites that cannot be read by screen readers.
**Cultural and language bias**: devices available only in English; facial recognition that works less accurately on darker skin.
**Economic bias**: expensive products that poorer communities cannot afford.

notes.label: Key idea
notes.text: **Inclusive (universal) design** aims to make products usable by as many people as possible: for example ramps, braille on lift buttons, adjustable seats and apps in all official languages.

items: Should we build something just because we can? Examples: surveillance cameras and privacy, genetically modified crops, social media data collection.
Products must be **safe**: tested, with warnings and instructions, and must follow standards (in South Africa, the **SABS**, South African Bureau of Standards).
**Intellectual property**: designers' ideas are protected by patents, copyright and trademarks.
Use renewable energy (solar, wind) and energy-efficient designs.
Choose materials that are recycled, recyclable or biodegradable.
Design products to last longer and to be repaired.
Consider the whole **life cycle**: raw materials → manufacture → use → disposal or recycling.

notes.text: When evaluating a product, ask: Does it meet the needs of the user? Is it safe? Is it affordable? Is it easy to use for different people? What are its environmental impacts? How could it be improved?

questions.prompt: Discuss TWO positive and TWO negative impacts of cellphones on society.
questions.memo:
Positive (1 each): communication; banking; learning; emergency help; jobs
Negative (1 each): cyberbullying; addiction; e-waste; distraction/accidents; privacy

questions.prompt: What is meant by the life cycle of a product?
questions.memo:
✓ All stages of the product's life (1)
✓ from raw materials and manufacture to use and disposal/recycling (1)

questions.prompt: Suggest THREE ways a designer can make a product more sustainable.
questions.memo: Any three (1 each): renewable energy; energy efficiency; recycled/recyclable materials; biodegradable materials; durable and repairable design; less packaging

questions.prompt: Give ONE advantage and ONE disadvantage of using robots in factories.
questions.memo:
✓ Advantage: faster / more accurate / safer for dangerous jobs / works continuously (1)
✓ Disadvantage: job losses / expensive / maintenance (1)

questions.prompt: Why might surveillance cameras in public places raise ethical questions?
